router.subject: Linguistics
router.title: Borrowed Words
paragraphs: No language is built entirely from its own materials. When speakers of different languages trade, travel, or live side by side, words pass from one language to another. Linguists call these words loanwords, although the term is slightly misleading, since a borrowed word is never given back.

Borrowing usually happens when a language lacks a name for something new. English speakers who first encountered foods such as sushi and yogurt simply adopted the Japanese and Turkish names along with the products. Borrowed words rarely stay unchanged, however. Their pronunciation is adjusted to fit the sound system of the new language, and their form may be shortened. In Japanese, for example, the English word "television" became terebi.

Not all borrowing fills a gap. After the Norman Conquest of 1066, French was the language of England's rulers, and thousands of French words entered English even where native words already existed. This is why the animals in the field are called cow and sheep, both Old English words, while the meat on the table is beef and mutton, both from French. Borrowing, in other words, reflects prestige as well as need, and a language's vocabulary is a record of the peoples its speakers have met.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: Why English has more words than most other languages
How the Norman Conquest changed English society
How and why words move from one language to another
Why borrowed words are difficult to pronounce
questions.why: Paragraph 1 defines loanwords, paragraph 2 explains borrowing out of need and paragraph 3 borrowing out of prestige.

questions.q: Why does the author describe the term "loanwords" as slightly misleading?
options: A loan is normally something that is returned.
Most loanwords are invented by the new language.
Linguists disagree about which words are loans.
Borrowed words usually change their meaning.
questions.why: The reason given is 'since a borrowed word is never given back': a real loan is returned, a loanword is not.

questions.q: The word "encountered" in the passage is closest in meaning to
options: learned to cook
wrote about
paid for
came across
questions.why: To encounter something is to meet or come across it; the speakers met these foods for the first time.

questions.q: According to the passage, what usually happens to a word after it is borrowed?
options: It replaces an older word that has the same meaning.
Its sound is changed to suit the new language.
It keeps its original spelling and sound.
It is returned to the original language.
questions.why: Paragraph 2: 'Their pronunciation is adjusted to fit the sound system of the new language.'

questions.q: Why does the author mention the words "beef" and "mutton"?
options: To show that French cooking became popular in England
To explain why some loanwords change their meaning
To give an example of borrowing without a real need
To prove that Old English had few words for food
questions.why: Paragraph 3 opens 'Not all borrowing fills a gap': French words came in 'even where native words already existed'.

upper.subject: Astronomy
upper.title: Detecting Distant Worlds
paragraphs: Astronomers long suspected that the Sun was not the only star with planets, but proof was slow to come. A planet shines only by reflected light, and that faint glow is drowned out by the star it circles. Seeing one directly is like trying to spot a firefly beside a lighthouse from many kilometers away. The first planet orbiting a Sun-like star was not confirmed until 1995.

Because direct observation is so difficult, most discoveries have relied on indirect evidence. One approach watches for a wobble: as a planet orbits, its gravity tugs the star slightly back and forth, and this motion subtly shifts the color of the star's light. Another, the transit method, monitors a star's brightness. If a planet happens to pass between the star and Earth, the light dims by a tiny fraction at regular intervals. Space telescopes using this technique have identified thousands of planets.

Neither method is neutral, however. A large planet close to its star produces a stronger wobble and deeper, more frequent dips in brightness than a small, distant one, so giant planets in tight orbits dominated the early lists. Astronomers therefore caution that the catalog reflects the limits of their instruments as much as the true population of planets. Worlds resembling Earth may be common; they are simply harder to detect.

questions.q: Why does the author mention a firefly and a lighthouse?
options: To explain how planets reflect the light of a star
To show how hard it is to see a planet near its star
To describe the instruments astronomers used before 1995
To suggest that most stars are brighter than the Sun
questions.why: The comparison follows 'that faint glow is drowned out by the star it circles': the firefly is the planet, the lighthouse the star.

questions.q: According to the passage, what does the transit method measure?
options: Slight changes in the color of a star's light
The glow reflected by a planet's surface
The distance between a star and Earth
Small, regular drops in a star's brightness
questions.why: The transit method 'monitors a star's brightness': 'the light dims by a tiny fraction at regular intervals'. Color shifts belong to the wobble method.

questions.q: The word "neutral" in the passage is closest in meaning to
options: unbiased
accurate
modern
simple
questions.why: The next sentence shows that both methods favor one kind of planet, so 'not neutral' means not unbiased.

questions.q: What can be inferred about a small planet that orbits far from its star?
options: It cannot have formed in the same way as Earth.
It reflects more light than a giant planet does.
It is more likely to be missed by both methods.
It causes its star to wobble more strongly.
questions.why: A small, distant planet gives a weaker wobble and shallower, rarer dips, so such worlds are 'simply harder to detect'.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: Why the first planet beyond the solar system was found only in 1995
How distant planets are found and why the results may be one-sided
Why planets like Earth are probably rare in the galaxy
How space telescopes have replaced observatories on the ground
questions.why: Paragraphs 1 and 2 explain the difficulty and the two indirect methods; paragraph 3 explains why the catalog 'reflects the limits of their instruments'.

Why the bookstore has changed its prices
What they must bring to the next lab
questions.why: 'Safety goggles are required for everyone. No goggles, no experiment.'

questions.q: Why does the professor mention that there are thirty students?
options: To explain why the lab will be divided into groups
To show that the spare goggles will not be enough
To complain that the class is too large
To remind students to arrive on time
questions.why: There are 'only six' spare pairs for thirty students: 'So please don't rely on those.'

router.subject: Psychology
router.script: Imagine you have a headache, and I give you a pill. Half an hour later, the pain is gone. Now, what if I told you that pill was made of sugar? Nothing in it at all. Would you believe me? Well, this happens all the time, and psychologists call it the placebo effect. A placebo is a treatment with no active ingredient. What does the work isn't the pill. It's your expectation that you're going to feel better. And here's the part I find fascinating. The details of the treatment matter. In experiments, people report more relief from two sugar pills than from one. A placebo they're told is expensive works better than one they think is cheap. So it's really the meaning we attach to the treatment that counts. Is it all imagination, then? Not exactly. When people expect pain relief, their brains actually release natural painkilling chemicals. So the change is real. But let's be careful here. Placebos mostly affect things we feel, like pain or tiredness. A sugar pill won't mend a broken bone. And this is exactly why researchers testing a new medicine give one group the real drug and another group a placebo. Only if the drug beats the placebo can they say it really works.

questions.q: What is the talk mainly about?
options: How researchers develop and produce new medicines
How expecting to improve can make people feel better
Why eating too much sugar can affect the brain
Why some patients refuse the treatment they are given
questions.why: The placebo effect: 'What does the work isn't the pill. It's your expectation that you're going to feel better.'

questions.q: What does the professor say about a placebo that people believe is expensive?
options: It usually contains some real medicine.
People refuse to take it.
It works only for headaches.
It gives more relief than a cheap one.
questions.why: 'A placebo they're told is expensive works better than one they think is cheap.'

questions.q: Why does the professor mention a broken bone?
options: To show that placebos have limits
To give an example of pain that placebos remove
To explain how natural painkillers are released
To describe an experiment with two groups
questions.why: 'Placebos mostly affect things we feel... A sugar pill won't mend a broken bone.'

questions.q: Why do researchers give a placebo to one group when they test a new medicine?
options: To save money on the real drug
To prevent the people in the study from feeling any pain
To see whether the drug works better than belief alone
To find out which people are easy to fool
questions.why: 'Only if the drug beats the placebo can they say it really works': the drug must do more than expectation does.

router.subject: Geography
router.script: OK, let's start with a little puzzle. In the Sahara, an afternoon can easily reach forty degrees Celsius. But stay there after dark, and the temperature may fall by twenty degrees or more. On a winter night, it can even come close to freezing. So where does all that heat go? Any ideas? Well, the short answer is: straight up. Let me explain. During the day, the ground soaks up energy from the sun. At night, it gives that energy back as heat, which escapes upward. Now, in most places, something keeps a lot of that heat from getting away. Water. Water vapor in the air and clouds overhead absorb the heat and send part of it back down. They work like a blanket. That's why a cloudy night usually feels milder than a clear one. But desert air is extremely dry, and the sky is almost always clear. There's no blanket. So the heat just leaks away into space. And there's a second reason. Sand itself. Sand warms up fast, but only the top layer gets hot, so it doesn't hold much heat, and it loses it quickly once the sun goes down. Compare that with a tropical rainforest. The air there is full of moisture, so the nights are only a little cooler than the days. Same sun, very different nights.

questions.q: What is the main topic of the talk?
options: How animals survive in the Sahara
Why deserts receive very little rain
Why desert nights are so cold
How clouds form over tropical forests
questions.why: The professor's puzzle is hot afternoons and cold nights in the Sahara: 'So where does all that heat go?'

questions.q: According to the professor, what do water vapor and clouds do at night?
options: They return some heat toward the ground.
They cool the air by blocking the sun.
They carry heat from deserts to forests.
They make the ground lose heat faster.
questions.why: They 'absorb the heat and send part of it back down. They work like a blanket.'

questions.q: What does the professor say about sand?
options: It reflects most of the sun's energy away.
It stores little heat and cools quickly.
It stays warm long after sunset.
It holds more water than soil does.
questions.why: 'It doesn't hold much heat, and it loses it quickly once the sun goes down.'

questions.q: Why does the professor mention a tropical rainforest?
options: To describe a place that gets less sunlight than a desert
To explain where desert moisture comes from
To give an example of a place with cold nights
To show what happens at night where the air is moist
questions.why: It is the contrast case: 'The air there is full of moisture, so the nights are only a little cooler than the days.'

upper.setting: Listen to an announcement from a university office.

Instead, you will be assigned a time slot according to the number of credits you have completed, with final-year students going first. Your slot will appear on your student portal by Monday. The Registrar's Office has too few employees.
Students were registering for more credits than allowed.
questions.why: 'The system crashed within minutes of opening, when several thousand students logged in at once. To avoid a repeat...'

questions.q: What can be inferred about a student who has completed few credits?
options: The student will not be able to register this term.
The student must register in person at the office.
The student will probably get a later time slot.
The student may log in early to save a place.
questions.why: Slots depend on credits completed, 'with final-year students going first', so fewer credits means a later slot.

upper.subject: Economics
upper.script: Picture a pasture that belongs to no one and is open to every herder in the village. Each herder asks a perfectly reasonable question: should I add one more cow? Well, the profit from that cow is mine alone. The damage it does to the grass, on the other hand, is shared by everybody. So I add the cow. And so does my neighbor, and hers. Before long, the pasture is bare, and everyone is worse off. In nineteen sixty-eight, the ecologist Garrett Hardin called this the tragedy of the commons, and you can see why the label stuck. Swap the pasture for the open ocean, and the cows for fishing boats, and you have a fair description of overfishing. Notice that nobody in the story is a villain. Each person acts sensibly, and together they wreck the thing they depend on. Hardin saw essentially two ways out: divide the resource into private property, or have the government regulate it. Now, that's where I think he was too gloomy. The political scientist Elinor Ostrom spent decades studying real communities, Swiss mountain villages sharing pastures, farmers sharing irrigation water, and she found that many had managed common resources for centuries. They made their own rules, kept an eye on one another, and punished cheats. So the tragedy is a real risk. It just isn't destiny.

questions.q: What is the talk mainly about?
options: How Swiss villages divide their land
Why fishing boats have become larger
How governments decide who should own a resource
Why shared resources risk being overused
questions.why: The pasture story, the overfishing example and Ostrom's findings all concern the tragedy of the commons.

questions.q: Why does the professor say that "nobody in the story is a villain"?
options: To suggest that the herders did not understand the problem
To stress that the harm comes from reasonable behavior
To defend Hardin against his critics
To show that the story is not based on real events
questions.why: She continues: 'Each person acts sensibly, and together they wreck the thing they depend on.'

questions.q: What is the professor's opinion of Hardin's two solutions?
options: They leave out a third possibility.
They have been proved to work everywhere.
They are too expensive to try.
They apply only to fishing.
questions.why: 'That's where I think he was too gloomy': Ostrom showed that communities can manage a resource themselves.

questions.q: According to the professor, what did Elinor Ostrom find?
options: Private owners protect resources better than villages do.
Most shared pastures disappeared centuries ago.
Some communities look after shared resources themselves.
Government rules are rarely obeyed.
questions.why: 'Many had managed common resources for centuries. They made their own rules, kept an eye on one another, and punished cheats.'

upper.subject: Marine biology
upper.script: Go down a thousand meters into the ocean, and the last trace of sunlight is gone. You'd expect total darkness. And yet, if you switch off your submarine's lights, the water around you flickers and sparkles. That's bioluminescence, light made by living things, and down there it's not the exception. It's the rule. The chemistry is fairly simple. A molecule called luciferin reacts with oxygen, with help from an enzyme, and the energy comes out as light instead of heat. What's more interesting is what the light is for. The anglerfish dangles a glowing lure in front of its mouth, and you can guess how that ends for a curious little fish. Some shrimp do the opposite. When attacked, they spit out a glowing cloud and slip away while the predator is dazzled. Then there's my favorite trick, and for this one we go a little higher, where a faint glow still filters down from the surface. The hatchetfish has lights along its belly. Odd place for them, isn't it? But seen from below, a fish is a dark shape against that glow. By lighting its belly to match, the hatchetfish erases its own shadow. It hides by shining. Most of this light is blue, because blue travels farthest through seawater. A few dragonfish, though, make red light, which most of their neighbors can't see at all. In effect, they hunt with a private flashlight.

questions.q: What is the talk mainly about?
options: How submarines explore the deep ocean
How and why deep-sea animals produce light
Why sunlight cannot reach the deep ocean floor
How anglerfish differ from hatchetfish
questions.why: The professor explains the chemistry of bioluminescence and then 'what the light is for'.

questions.q: What does the professor imply when he says "you can guess how that ends for a curious little fish"?
options: The small fish is eaten.
The small fish learns to avoid light.
The small fish steals the lure.
The small fish begins to glow.
questions.why: The glowing lure hangs 'in front of its mouth', so a fish that comes to look becomes a meal.

questions.q: Why does the hatchetfish have lights on its belly?
options: To attract smaller fish swimming below it
To warn other hatchetfish of danger
To hide its outline from animals below
To find its way in total darkness
questions.why: 'By lighting its belly to match, the hatchetfish erases its own shadow. It hides by shining.'

questions.q: Why does the professor call the dragonfish's red light "a private flashlight"?
options: Because red light travels farther than blue light
Because dragonfish live alone
Because the light is too weak to be useful
Because most other animals cannot see it
questions.why: The red light is something 'most of their neighbors can't see at all', so only the dragonfish benefits from it.

email.scenario: You want to apply for a six-week summer program in science journalism at another university. The application requires a recommendation letter from a professor, and the deadline is only ten days away. Last semester you took Professor Haddad's news writing course and received a high grade on your final article. You decide to write to Professor Haddad to ask for a letter.
email.subject: Request for a recommendation letter
bullets: Explain why you want to attend the program.
Describe the work you did in Professor Haddad's course.
Ask for the letter and say when it is needed.
email.model:
Dear Professor Haddad,

I hope you are well. I am writing to ask whether you would be willing to write a recommendation letter for me.

I am applying to the Summer Program in Science Journalism at Northgate University. I hope to become a science reporter, and the program would let me practice interviewing researchers and writing for a real student magazine.

I took your News Writing course last semester. For my final project, I wrote an article about water quality in the campus lake, and you kindly said that it was clear and carefully researched. I learned a great deal from your comments on my drafts.

I am sorry for the short notice, but the letter must be uploaded by March 20, which is ten days from now. I have attached my résumé and the program description. Please let me know if you need anything else.

Thank you very much for considering my request.

Sincerely,
Linh Tran

professor.name: Dr. Marchetti
professor.post: This week we are looking at policies designed to reduce plastic waste. Many governments have targeted single-use plastic bags, but they have chosen different tools. Some, such as Kenya and Rwanda, have banned the bags completely. Others, such as Ireland, require stores to charge customers a small fee for each bag. Both approaches aim to change shoppers' habits. Which do you think is the better policy: banning single-use plastic bags or charging a fee for them? Why?

students.name: Yusuf
students.post: I think a ban is better because it is simple and it works immediately. When a fee is small, many shoppers just pay it and keep using plastic bags, especially people with higher incomes. A ban treats everyone the same way. After a few weeks, bringing a reusable bag becomes a normal habit, just like bringing a wallet.

students.name: Greta
students.post: I prefer a fee. A ban removes people's choice, and sometimes a plastic bag is really necessary, for example when you buy fresh fish or forget your own bag. A fee still makes people think twice, and the money collected can pay for recycling programs or beach cleanups. A ban produces no money at all for the environment.

discussion.model: I believe that charging a fee is the better policy, as long as the fee is high enough to matter. Yusuf is right that a very small charge is easy to ignore, but that is an argument for raising the price, not for a ban. Greta mentions that the money can support recycling, and I would add another advantage: a fee is much easier to enforce. When bags are banned completely, some shops keep handing them out secretly, and inspectors must visit every market to stop them. With a fee, stores simply record each bag at the cash register, so the rule is followed almost automatically. Finally, a fee can be adjusted. If people are still using too many bags after a year, the government can increase the charge step by step until the habit really changes.

interview.scenario: You have agreed to take part in a research study about travel and vacations. You will have a short online interview with a researcher. The researcher will ask you some questions.

questions.q: Thank you for taking part in this study. Let's start with your own experience. Please tell me about a trip you took that you remember well. Where did you go, and what made it memorable?
questions.model: A trip I remember very well is a visit to my grandparents' village two summers ago. I went with my cousin, and we traveled by train for almost nine hours. The village is in the mountains, so the air was cool and clean, which was a big change from the city. What made the trip memorable was how simple each day was. We helped my grandfather pick apples in the morning, swam in the river in the afternoon, and listened to his stories at night. There was almost no phone signal, so nobody looked at a screen. I came home feeling completely rested.

questions.q: Some people like to plan every detail of a vacation in advance, while others prefer to decide what to do after they arrive. Which kind of traveler are you, and why?
questions.model: I am definitely a planner, although I leave a little free time. Before a trip, I book my transportation and my accommodation, and I make a short list of places I really want to see. The main reason is money. Tickets and rooms are usually cheaper when you reserve them early, and as a student I have to be careful with my budget. Planning also saves time, because I don't spend half a morning deciding where to go. However, I never fill the whole schedule. I always keep one afternoon open, since the best moments often happen when you simply walk around without a plan.

questions.q: Now I'd like to ask for your opinion. Some people say that you learn more by traveling to another country than by reading or watching videos about it. Do you agree or disagree? Why?
questions.model: I mostly agree. Books and videos can give you facts, but they are chosen and edited by someone else, so you only see what that person wants to show. When you travel, you notice small things that nobody films, such as how people wait in line, how loudly they speak, or what they eat for breakfast. You also have to solve real problems, like buying a ticket in another language, and that teaches you a lot. On the other hand, a short trip can give a false picture, because tourists usually see only the most famous places. So I think travel teaches more, but only if you stay long enough and talk to local people.

questions.q: Here is my final question. Popular tourist destinations sometimes become so crowded that daily life gets harder for the people who live there. Do you think cities should limit the number of tourists who can visit? Why or why not?
questions.model: Yes, I think cities should be able to limit tourist numbers when it is really necessary. In very popular places, residents face higher rents, crowded buses, and noise late at night, and some of them finally move away. If that continues, the city loses the local life that made it attractive in the first place. However, I would not close the city to visitors. A better method is to control the busiest places and times, for example by selling a fixed number of tickets for a famous square or museum each day. Cities can also encourage people to come in the quiet season. In this way, tourism still supports local jobs without making life unpleasant for residents.
